v-collocation-14.reason: A passport is 'valid' for six months after entry. effective (documents/laws take effect, a passport is not 'effective for six months'), active (accounts, not passports) and legal (a document is not 'legal for a period') are not standard with a passport and a validity period.
v-collocation-14.ldbs: L yes (effective reads fine in 'will not be ___ for at least six months'); D yes (the subject 'passports' is twenty words back, behind a which-clause); B no (no good student believes effective/active/legal); S no. Medium = L plus D.
v-collocation-14.why: Medium: effective passes the local window and the subject is far away, but nobody actively believes the distractors (B fails).
v-collocation-14.editorNote: valid + passport + six months is the stock rule. The long which-clause pushes the subject away but adds no real difficulty. Style is 4 because the stem is a little bureaucratic.

v-collocation-15.reason: 'in urgent need of repair' is the fixed collocation. 'in rapid / prompt / hasty need' are not English; rapid, prompt and hasty describe speed of action, not need.
v-collocation-15.ldbs: L fails: 'in ___ need of' admits only urgent; rapid/prompt/hasty are dead on arrival in the window. D, B and S also no.
v-collocation-15.why: Easy: L fails. The fixed phrase 'in ___ need of' eliminates every distractor locally, however long the stem is.
v-collocation-15.fix: Distractors need to be locally viable. Change the frame so the three speed words can sit in the window, e.g. 'the report calls for ___ repair of the cracked ramp' with action/attention words, or choose a collocation where the distractors modify the same noun. Alternatively use pressing / critical / immediate as options (and watch ambiguity).
v-collocation-15.editorNote: The two relative-clause insertions only add length; they do not hide the clue. The batch has three items built on a long 'which' insertion.

v-collocation-16.reason: 'poorly attended' is the stock collocation. 'hardly attended' (scarcely) cannot take 'so ... that' here, 'weakly attended' and 'mildly attended' are not used. 'so hardly attended' is ungrammatical in the degree frame.
v-collocation-16.ldbs: L fails: in 'so ___ attended' only poorly reads naturally. D, B and S no.
v-collocation-16.why: Easy: L fails. 'poorly attended' is a fixed pair and the other three adverbs are not locally acceptable.
v-collocation-16.fix: Replace mildly / weakly with adverbs that can truly stand next to 'attended' or an adjective in this frame (sparsely, thinly, barely) to give a local distractor; check that none of them becomes a second answer (sparsely attended is also standard).
v-collocation-16.editorNote: Both mildly and weakly are close to filler distractors. The consequence clause (canceled the afternoon session) reads like a hint but it does not matter because the collocation decides.

v-collocation-17.reason: 'trip hazard' is a fixed compound. 'trip danger', 'trip harm' and 'trip threat' are not used.
v-collocation-17.ldbs: L fails: 'a trip ___' admits only hazard (the fixed compound). D, B and S no.
v-collocation-17.why: Easy: L fails. Compound noun fixed immediately adjacent to the gap; the safety officer clause is not needed.
v-collocation-17.fix: To raise it, move the compound partner away from the gap (e.g. 'The cable presents a ___ that the safety officer ... because staff could trip over it' is too definitional; better pick another collocation family where the distractors are viable).
v-collocation-17.editorNote: hazard is also the first synonym a learner would think of for 'safety officer' context, so the answer is guessable even without the compound. danger could pass as a loose compound ('a trip danger') in some informal safety signage, but it is not standard.

v-synonym-14.reason: 'inquire whether' takes a whether-clause. request takes an object or that-clause (not 'whether'), insist takes that, demand takes that or 'to know whether'; none takes a bare whether-clause. 'requested ..., whether' and 'demanded ..., whether' are not accepted in formal writing (demanded whether is archaic at best).
v-synonym-14.ldbs: L yes (requested/demanded read fine in 'have since ___, by telephone and by e-mail,'); D yes (the whether-clause is after the inserted 'by telephone and by e-mail'); B weak (requested is somewhat believable, but 'requested whether' is rarely something a good student confidently believes); S no. Medium.
v-synonym-14.why: Medium: L and D pass, B is only weak. The complement type (whether) is the decider, not a trap good students trust.
v-synonym-14.fix: To make it hard, add a distractor that takes whether in a real but different use, or make the complement a that-clause vs whether so more than one option is locally believed. Alternatively keep and accept medium.
v-synonym-14.editorNote: insisted and demanded are near-throwaway distractors because both normally take that. 'asked' is deliberately absent; fine. Check no other item in the batch uses 'inquired' as a distractor.

v-synonym-15.reason: 'vacate the unit' is the lease term: leave it empty and return the keys. evict and expel need a person as object (the tenant cannot evict the unit). evacuate fits the grammar and a loose 'leave' meaning, but it implies removal from danger/emergency; nothing in the sentence gives one (the repairs are routine), so an editor would change it to vacate.
v-synonym-15.ldbs: L yes (evacuate reads fine locally: 'must evacuate the unit and hand all keys'); D weak (lease clues 'last day of the contract' are after the gap but the exclusion of evacuate rests on the missing emergency, not a distant clue); B yes (evacuate is believed as a synonym of leave; this is a different true usage); S no. Medium by the rule L + B; D is not clean.
v-synonym-15.why: Medium: L passes and B passes (evacuate), but the exclusion is by sense nuance rather than a distant clue, so D is not clean enough for hard.
v-synonym-15.fix: To protect against evacuate: add a non-emergency detail near the gap (e.g. 'once the lease expires' next to the verb) or replace evacuate with a verb that is clearly wrong for a unit (e.g. 'evaluate', 'elevate') if a family distractor is wanted. If evacuate is kept, expect some editors to accept the loose sense.
v-synonym-15.editorNote: evacuate is a near miss: needs an emergency assumption the stem does not give. Some US/UK lease language does use 'evacuate the premises' loosely, but standard usage keeps evacuate for danger or orders. Listed in shouldFix. Two items in this batch use lease/tenant scenes (synonym-14 and synonym-15).

v-synonym-16.reason: 'mislead X into believing' is the standard frame. misinform takes about/of or a that-clause, not 'into'; misdirect means send the wrong way (traffic, funds, efforts) and is not used with 'into believing'; misplace means lose. 'misinformed into believing' appears occasionally in the wild but copy editors change it to misled, and the wording here is ambiguous, not false, which fits mislead and not misinform.
v-synonym-16.ldbs: L yes (misinform reads perfectly in 'may misinform customers, particularly those who glance only at the large type'); D yes ('into believing' arrives after the insertion, about ten words past the gap); B yes (misinform is a real near-synonym good students trust; the difference is the 'into' frame and the true/false nuance); S yes (ignore the insertion to see the object-into frame). Hard.
v-synonym-16.why: Hard: L, D, B and S all pass. The 'into' frame is far from the gap and misinform is a believable near-synonym.
v-synonym-16.editorNote: misinform is the near miss: 'misinform X into Ving' is rare but not unattested. An editor would almost certainly change it, so not ambiguous. If a stricter reviewer disagrees, swap misinform for misguide-free alternative such as 'mistake' or 'misquote'. misplace is a throwaway distractor.

v-synonym-17.reason: 'interfere with' is the verb + preposition frame the 'with' after the insertion demands. disturb and interrupt are transitive (disturb/interrupt the sessions), so 'disturb, ..., with the sessions' and 'interrupt, ..., with the sessions' are ungrammatical. 'intervene with' is not used for machinery affecting an activity (intervene in/between). 'intervene with' in the sense of approach someone does not fit either.
v-synonym-17.ldbs: L yes (all four read fine in 'allowed to ___, as it did twice'); D yes ('with' comes after the inserted 'as it did twice last month'); B yes (disturb and interrupt are meaning-correct synonyms a good student trusts; the failure is the preposition); S yes (strip the inserted clause to see verb + with). Hard.
v-synonym-17.why: Hard: all four questions pass. The preposition that decides the verb is separated from the gap by an insertion, and two distractors are exactly right in meaning.
v-synonym-17.editorNote: Very good item: synonym trap decided by a distant preposition. intervene is a pure family distractor and nothing in the sentence supports it. Confirm this is the only item in the batch where a split verb + preposition decides.

v-business-12.reason: The subcontractor billed too much: 'overcharged the company by $12,000 for materials never delivered'. overpaid has the wrong direction (the company paid; the subcontractor was paid, so 'overpaid the company' is impossible), overspent takes a budget/amount and no person object, overdrawn applies to accounts and is not used with an agent + object + 'by'.
v-business-12.ldbs: L yes (overpaid is locally excellent: 'the company had been paying ... had overpaid the company'); D yes (the true subject 'the subcontractor' is twelve words before the gap behind a whose-clause); B yes (direction error: overcharge vs overpay, which good students trust); S yes (find the real subject across the insertion to judge direction). Hard.
v-business-12.why: Hard: the near distractor is overpaid (direction trap); the whose-clause makes 'the company' look like the subject, and the subject is separated from the gap.
v-business-12.editorNote: 'overcharged ... for materials that were never delivered' is slightly loose (charging for goods never supplied is more like billing falsely) but it is acceptable and no option fits better. overspent and overdrawn are weak distractors; only overpaid really carries the item.

v-business-13.reason: 'staff turnover' is the HR metric (rate of people leaving) and the cut recruitment budget follows from it. 'staff turnout' means attendance at an event; turnaround is processing time; takeover is an acquisition. None gives a rate that falls and justifies a smaller recruitment budget.
v-business-13.ldbs: L yes, barely ('staff turnout at the call center has fallen from 31 percent to 14 percent' reads passably as attendance); D yes ('the recruitment budget has been cut accordingly' comes at the end and excludes turnout, because lower attendance would not cut recruitment); B no (nobody confidently believes turnout); S no. Medium by the rule, but close to the easy edge.
v-business-13.why: Medium: L passes only barely (turnout is a local fit) and D yes, B no. 'staff turnover' is a stock compound, so this is the lowest medium in the batch.
v-business-13.fix: To make it clearly medium, give turnout a real chance by dropping 'staff' as the pre-modifier, or use options such as attrition / turnover / absenteeism / turnout that are all HR words.
v-business-13.editorNote: Frequency is fine and the clue is not a definition. A strict reviewer could call this easy because 'staff turnover' is instant for most test-takers; I keep medium only because of 'turnout' and the 31 to 14 percent figures.

v-business-14.reason: A patent protects how an invention works and stops others from manufacturing it. copyright protects expression (text, images) and cannot stop a valve from being made, trademark protects a brand identifier, license is permission, and none of them is 'filed for a valve design so that competitors cannot make a valve that works the same way'.
v-business-14.ldbs: L yes ('filed a copyright for the new valve design' / 'filed a trademark' read locally, and design suggests copyright); D yes (the so-that clause that excludes them is after the gap); B no (copyright for a mechanism is not something a good student confidently believes); S no. The so-that clause comes close to defining a patent, so medium at most.
v-business-14.why: Medium: L and D pass, B fails, and the tail 'competitors could not manufacture a valve that works in the same way' nearly defines patent.
v-business-14.fix: Remove or soften the explanatory tail ('so that competitors could not manufacture...') into something that still needs a step, e.g. 'ahead of the fair, once the supplier tooling was ordered'.
v-business-14.editorNote: 'file a copyright' is not standard (one registers copyright), and 'file a trademark' is only loose speech (file a trademark application). Neither is defensible against a functional design. Stem tail is close to a definition of patent (warning per 6.1 'definition' rule).

v-family-11.reason: A lockout check must come before inspection: 'precede'. succeed (follow) reverses direction and is excluded by 'before any maintenance work begins ... so'. proceed (go on; 'proceed with / to') cannot take 'the first inspection' as direct object; 'proceed the inspection' is a known slip for precede, which editors correct. exceed means go beyond and does not fit.
v-family-11.ldbs: L yes (succeed reads fine: 'a lockout check must always succeed the first inspection'; proceed is a familiar slip); D yes ('before any maintenance work begins' and the 'so' logic come before the gap, in the first clause); B yes (precede/succeed direction trap and the proceed/precede confusion are exactly what good students get wrong); S no. Hard by the rule L + D + B.
v-family-11.why: Hard: L, D and B pass. succeed is locally perfect and is excluded only by the order logic in the first clause.
v-family-11.fix: Make the order logic a touch less dependent on background: 'before any maintenance work begins' plus 'so' reads that the inspection belongs to maintenance, which the sentence only implies. Consider 'before any maintenance work, including the first inspection, begins'? no (too definitional); better keep and add 'the first step of any maintenance visit'.
v-family-11.editorNote: The direction reasoning assumes the first inspection counts as maintenance work ('so' signals it but does not state it). A strict reader can say succeed is logically odd rather than impossible; I do not count it as ambiguous because 'so' ties the clause to the earlier before-statement. Raised for the fixer to confirm. proceed is also a real learner confusion with precede.

v-family-12.reason: 'defective when it left the factory' is the product-warranty term. deficient needs 'in something' (deficient in iron) or describes inadequate quantity or quality; the absolute use 'was deficient' for an appliance is occasionally seen but editors would change it to defective. defiant and defensive are people attitudes.
v-family-12.ldbs: L yes (deficient reads acceptably in 'because it was deficient when it left the factory'); D weak (clues are 'stops working within twelve months' and 'replaced free of charge', both before the gap or well after it, but the exclusion rests on collocation, not on a distant clue); B yes (deficient is a believable cousin of defective); S no. Medium; the stem 'stops working because it was ___' partly defines defective.
v-family-12.why: Medium: L and B pass; D is soft and the stem 'stops working because it was ___' leans on the meaning of defective.
v-family-12.fix: Replace deficient, which is the near miss, with a family word that cannot stand for faulty (e.g. definitive or defunct is risky; definite is safe) so the item rests on defective vs defensive/defiant, or keep deficient and add a clue such as 'in iron-free alloys' that excludes it.
v-family-12.editorNote: deficient is close to acceptable: 'deficient products / deficient design' appears in product-liability English. Needs no extra assumption, so it only just misses ambiguity. Listed in shouldFix.

v-family-13.reason: 'occupancy' is the capacity set by fire codes, limited 'to 180 guests'. occupation means the act of occupying (or a job); 'limited the occupation of the room to 180 guests' is stretched and an editor would change it. occupant and occupier are people (you cannot limit 'the occupant of a room to 180 guests').
v-family-13.ldbs: L yes, barely ('limited the occupation of its second-floor banquet room' reads acceptably in the window); D yes ('to 180 guests' and 'fire code' decide, and sit outside the four-word window); B no (nobody confidently believes occupation here); S no. Medium, near the easy edge.
v-family-13.why: Medium: L passes only through occupation, D passes ('to 180 guests'), B fails. 'fire code ... occupancy' is also a stock link.
v-family-13.editorNote: occupation is a near miss in a legal or British sense ('occupation of premises'), but it does not give 'capacity'; not ambiguous. The stem uses 'fire code' and '180 guests', both of which lead to occupancy, which keeps this near the easy edge. Style 4.

shouldFix: v-synonym-15: evacuate is a near miss (loose 'leave' sense, no emergency in the stem); add a non-emergency cue near the gap or replace evacuate with a family word that clearly fails.
v-family-12: deficient is a near miss in product-liability English; replace it with a family word that cannot stand for faulty, or add a clue that excludes it.
overall: No second answer survives 4.1 in any of the 14 items, so mustFix is empty. Bands: 3 easy (collocation-15, -16, -17), 7 medium (collocation-14, synonym-14, synonym-15, business-13, business-14, family-12, family-13), 4 hard (synonym-16, synonym-17, business-12, family-11). That gives 21% easy, 50% medium, 29% hard, against the 5.2 target of at most 20% easy and at least 30% hard: only just short on hard and one item over on easy. Four of the seven mediums (business-13, business-14, family-13, collocation-14) sit close to the easy edge because the L pass is marginal or the stem nearly gives the stock phrase away. The best items are synonym-17 and business-12, where a meaning-correct distractor is excluded by a distant preposition or a distant subject. The three collocation items (15, 16, 17) are all easy: the answer is a fixed phrase adjacent to the gap and the distractors are dead locally, so they should be rebuilt on collocations whose distractors are locally viable. Batch notes: two lease or tenant scenes (synonym-14, synonym-15); loading dock or area in collocation-15 and synonym-17; four stems use a mid-sentence which/whose insertion; no correct answer appears as a distractor elsewhere in the batch; none looks like a known real item.
